questions.stem: In the model of ionic bonding, what holds a crystal of sodium chloride together?
options: Weak forces of attraction between NaCl molecules
Attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice
Shared pairs of electrons between sodium and chlorine atoms
Delocalised electrons moving between positive sodium ions
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by electrostatic attraction between opposite charges. There are no NaCl molecules and no shared electron pairs; delocalised electrons describe metallic bonding.

questions.stem: Solid potassium bromide does not conduct electricity, but molten potassium bromide does. Why?
options: Melting breaks covalent bonds to form charged atoms
The solid has no ions until it is heated strongly
In the melt the ions are free to move and carry charge
Melting releases delocalised electrons from the lattice
questions.explanation: The solid contains ions, but they are fixed in the lattice. When it melts (or dissolves) the ions can move, so they carry the current; ionic compounds have no delocalised electrons.

questions.stem: Why does an ionic crystal shatter when it is struck with a hammer?
options: The covalent bonds inside each ion are broken by the blow
Layers shift so that ions of the same charge line up and repel
The delocalised electrons are knocked out of the lattice
The weak forces between neighbouring molecules are overcome
questions.explanation: A blow moves one layer of ions relative to the next, bringing like charges side by side. Their repulsion splits the crystal, which is why ionic solids are brittle rather than malleable.

questions.stem: Why do ionic compounds such as magnesium oxide have high melting points?
options: The delocalised electrons must first be removed
The molecules are large and tangled together
Many strong attractions between ions must be overcome
Strong covalent bonds inside each molecule must be broken
questions.explanation: Melting an ionic solid means freeing ions from a lattice held by strong electrostatic attraction in every direction, which needs a lot of energy. Ionic compounds are not made of molecules.

questions.stem: Which of these substances is made up of discrete molecules?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is covalent molecular: separate CO₂ molecules with weak forces between them. Sodium chloride is an ionic lattice, copper a metallic lattice and diamond a covalent network, none of which has separate molecules.

questions.stem: Which description fits the model of bonding in a solid metal such as aluminium?
options: Neutral atoms held together by weak intermolecular forces
Positive ions in a regular arrangement held by delocalised electrons
Positive and negative ions held in a lattice by opposite charges
Atoms sharing pairs of electrons in fixed covalent bonds
questions.explanation: A metal is modelled as a lattice of cations stabilised by attraction to a sea of delocalised electrons that are free to move. A lattice of positive and negative ions describes an ionic compound.

questions.stem: Why can copper be drawn into wires without breaking?
options: The ions repel each other strongly, so they spread out into a thin wire shape
The covalent bonds between copper atoms bend without breaking when stretched
The copper molecules are long chains that can be pulled out straight
The ions can slide past each other while the delocalised electrons keep holding them
questions.explanation: When a force is applied, layers of cations slide over each other, and the delocalised electrons move with them so the attraction is not lost. This makes metals malleable and ductile, unlike brittle ionic solids.

questions.stem: Which feature of metallic bonding explains why metals conduct electricity in the solid state?
options: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice
Positive ions move towards the negative terminal
Negative ions move towards the positive terminal
Shared electron pairs jump from bond to bond
questions.explanation: Current in a metal is a flow of the delocalised electrons. The metal ions stay in fixed positions in the lattice, and there are no negative ions in a pure metal.

questions.stem: When water boils, which forces are overcome?
options: The bonds holding the nucleus together
The O−H bonds within each molecule
The forces between hydrogen and oxygen ions
questions.explanation: Boiling separates molecules from each other by overcoming intermolecular forces. The covalent O−H bonds inside each molecule are much stronger and stay intact, so steam is still H₂O.

questions.stem: Iodine, I₂, is a solid that turns to a vapour on gentle heating, yet the I−I bond is strong. Which statement explains this?
options: Iodine atoms lose their delocalised electrons when heated, so the lattice collapses
Intermolecular forces are weak, so molecules separate without breaking the I−I bonds
The I−I covalent bonds break easily, so the solid falls apart into separate iodine atoms
Iodine is an ionic solid, and its ions escape from the lattice when it is heated
questions.explanation: Covalent molecular substances have strong bonds within molecules (intramolecular) but weak forces between molecules (intermolecular). Turning to a vapour only overcomes the weak forces between I₂ molecules.

questions.stem: Which property is typical of covalent molecular substances such as methane and sulfur?
options: Low melting point and no electrical conduction
High melting point and conduction when molten
Malleability and conduction in the solid state
High melting point and great hardness
questions.explanation: Weak intermolecular forces give low melting points, and with no free ions or electrons they do not conduct. Conduction when molten is ionic behaviour, and great hardness belongs to covalent networks.

questions.stem: How many bonds does a carbon atom form in diamond, and what does this explain?
options: Four, giving a rigid network that makes diamond very hard
Three, leaving a free electron that makes diamond conduct
Two, forming chains that make diamond flexible
Four, forming separate small molecules that make diamond soft
questions.explanation: Each carbon in diamond is covalently bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network, so a huge number of strong bonds must break to scratch or melt it. Three bonds per carbon describes graphite.

questions.stem: Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not?
options: Graphite contains carbon ions that can move between its layers
Graphite's carbon atoms are held together by metallic bonds
Diamond's electrons are delocalised but cannot pass between crystals
Each carbon in graphite bonds to three others, leaving one electron delocalised
questions.explanation: In graphite each carbon forms three covalent bonds within a layer, and the fourth outer electron is delocalised along the layer and can carry current. In diamond all four outer electrons are in bonds, so none are free.

questions.stem: Graphite is used in pencils because it leaves marks on paper. Which feature of its structure explains this?
options: Its separate C₆₀ molecules rub off one at a time
Weak forces between layers allow the layers to slide off
Strong bonds between layers hold flakes together on paper
Delocalised electrons make the graphite stick to paper
questions.explanation: Graphite is made of flat layers of carbon atoms with only weak forces between the layers, so layers slide off and stay on the paper. C₆₀ molecules describe a fullerene, not graphite.

questions.stem: Which statement describes fullerenes such as C₆₀?
options: They are three-dimensional networks of carbon like diamond
They are flat sheets of carbon stacked in weakly held layers
They are ionic compounds of carbon with a metal
They are molecules of carbon atoms arranged in hollow cage shapes
questions.explanation: Fullerenes are allotropes of carbon made of discrete molecules, such as the ball-shaped C₆₀. Because they are molecules rather than giant networks, their properties differ from both diamond and graphite.

questions.stem: Substance W melts at about 1700 °C, does not conduct as a solid or liquid, and is insoluble in water. Which structure is it most likely to have?
questions.explanation: A very high melting point with no conduction even when molten points to a covalent network such as silicon dioxide. An ionic solid would conduct when molten, a metal would conduct as a solid, and a molecular substance would melt at a low temperature.

questions.stem: Substance V melts at 801 °C, conducts only when molten or dissolved, and its solid is brittle. Which structure is it most likely to have?
questions.explanation: Conducting when molten or in solution but not as a solid shows that V contains ions that are fixed in the solid and free in the liquid. Brittleness and a high melting point also fit an ionic lattice.

questions.stem: What is the formula of the sulfate ion?
questions.explanation: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. SO₃²⁻ is sulfite, and S²⁻ is the sulfide ion.

questions.stem: What is the formula of calcium nitrate?
questions.explanation: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻, so two nitrate ions balance one calcium ion. Brackets show that the whole nitrate group is doubled; NO₂⁻ is nitrite.

questions.stem: What is the name of Al₂(SO₄)₃?
questions.explanation: Al₂(SO₄)₃ contains Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions. Ionic compounds are named without numerical prefixes, and the -ate ending identifies sulfate rather than sulfide (S²⁻) or sulfite (SO₃²⁻).

questions.stem: Ammonium ions and phosphate ions combine to form a salt. What is its formula?
questions.explanation: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and phosphate is PO₄³⁻, so three ammonium ions balance one phosphate ion. (NH₄)₂PO₄ would leave the compound with an overall charge of 1−.

questions.stem: Iron forms Fe³⁺ ions in iron(III) oxide. What is the formula of this compound?
questions.explanation: The Roman numeral shows the iron ion is Fe³⁺, and oxide is O²⁻. The lowest whole-number ratio with zero overall charge is 2 Fe³⁺ (6+) to 3 O²⁻ (6−). FeO is iron(II) oxide.

questions.stem: What is the name of the covalent compound PCl₅?
questions.explanation: Covalent molecular compounds use prefixes for the number of each atom: penta- means five. The prefix mono- is not used on the first element.

questions.stem: What is the formula of dinitrogen tetroxide?
questions.explanation: Di- means two nitrogen atoms and tetr(a)- means four oxygen atoms, so the formula is N₂O₄. NO₂ is nitrogen dioxide and N₂O₅ is dinitrogen pentoxide.

questions.stem: In the electron dot diagram of a water molecule, how many bonding pairs and non-bonding (lone) pairs surround the oxygen atom?
questions.explanation: Oxygen has 6 outer electrons; it shares 2 with the hydrogen atoms to form 2 bonding pairs, and the remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs. That gives oxygen a full outer shell of 8 electrons.

questions.stem: How many pairs of electrons are shared between the atoms in an electron dot diagram of carbon dioxide, O=C=O?
questions.explanation: Each C=O double bond is 2 shared pairs, and there are two double bonds, so 4 pairs are shared. Carbon's 4 outer electrons and 2 from each oxygen give carbon a full shell of 8 electrons.

questions.stem: How many shared pairs of electrons join the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
questions.explanation: Each nitrogen atom has 5 outer electrons and needs 3 more, so the atoms share 3 pairs in a triple bond. Each nitrogen then also has one lone pair.

questions.stem: Water (molar mass 18 g/mol) boils at 100 °C, while methane (16 g/mol) boils at about −162 °C. What explains the difference?
options: Water molecules contain stronger covalent bonds than methane
Water is an ionic compound, while methane is covalent
Water molecules are much heavier than methane molecules
Water molecules are highly polar, so they attract each other strongly
questions.explanation: The two molecules have similar masses, but water is highly polar, so the attraction between its molecules is much stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Boiling does not break covalent bonds, and water is molecular, not ionic.

questions.stem: Valency is the number of bonds an atom can form. Phosphorus is 2, 8, 5. What is the formula of the simplest compound of phosphorus and hydrogen?
questions.explanation: Phosphorus has 5 outer electrons and needs 3 more, so its valency is 3, and each hydrogen has a valency of 1. Three hydrogen atoms bond to one phosphorus atom, giving PH₃.

questions.stem: A gas makes a lit splint go out with a squeaky pop. Which gas is it?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen burns rapidly with oxygen in air, giving the squeaky pop. Oxygen relights a glowing splint, and carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

questions.stem: Which test identifies carbon dioxide?
options: It burns with a squeaky pop
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) to form a white precipitate of calcium carbonate. Relighting a glowing splint is the test for oxygen.

questions.stem: In a flame test, why does each metal ion give a characteristic colour?
options: Its electrons are excited and emit light of particular energies as they return
The ion burns in oxygen to form a coloured metal oxide
The heat breaks the ion's nucleus apart and releases coloured light
The flame dissolves the ion and colours the gases above it
questions.explanation: Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels, and when they fall back they emit light of energies that depend on the element's electron arrangement. Nuclear changes are not involved in a flame test.

questions.stem: Solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride are mixed and a white precipitate forms. What is the net ionic equation?
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is insoluble, so it precipitates; the net ionic equation shows only the ions that react. Sodium nitrate is soluble, and the full equation including Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ is the overall equation, not the net ionic one.

questions.stem: Barium chloride solution is added to sodium sulfate solution. Which ions are spectator ions?
questions.explanation: Barium sulfate is insoluble, so Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine to form the precipitate. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved and unchanged, so they are spectator ions.

questions.stem: Using the solubility rules, which pair of solutions forms a precipitate when mixed?
questions.explanation: Copper(II) hydroxide is insoluble, so a precipitate forms. In the other pairs every possible product contains a group 1 or ammonium ion or a nitrate ion, so all stay in solution.

questions.stem: Lead(II) nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution and a yellow precipitate forms. What is the balanced net ionic equation?
questions.explanation: Lead(II) iodide is insoluble and contains Pb²⁺, so two iodide ions are needed to balance each lead ion. K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions, since potassium nitrate is soluble.

questions.stem: An unknown colourless solution is one of NaCl, Na₂SO₄ or NaNO₃. Adding barium nitrate solution gives a white precipitate. Which compound is present?
questions.explanation: Barium sulfate is insoluble, so a white precipitate with barium ions shows sulfate. Barium chloride and barium nitrate are both soluble, so NaCl and NaNO₃ would give no precipitate.

questions.stem: Three unlabelled solutions are KNO₃, Ba(NO₃)₂ and Mg(NO₃)₂. Sodium sulfate gives a precipitate with only one of them, and sodium carbonate gives a precipitate with two. Which solution gave a precipitate with both reagents?
questions.explanation: Barium sulfate is insoluble while magnesium sulfate is soluble, so only barium precipitates with sulfate. Barium and magnesium carbonates are both insoluble, so the barium solution is the only one that precipitates with both; potassium salts are all soluble.
